claims.text: What the image looks like Buzzword: double bubble on newborn AXR → duodenal atresia (associated with Down syndrome)
claims.quote: Double bubble AXR (newborn) Duodenal atresia (associated with Down syndrome)

claims.text: Double-bubble sign of complete duodenal obstruction: the smaller bubble is the proximal, dilated duodenum; the larger bubble is the stomach
claims.quote: This radiograph shows the typical double-bubble sign seen with complete duodenal obstruction. The smaller bubble represents the proximal, dilated duodenum (white arrow); the larger bubble represents the stomach (black arrow).

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Classic radiograph: one bubble in the stomach, the other in the proximal duodenum, and little to no air in the distal gut
claims.quote: The diagnosis is suspected by symptoms and classic double-bubble radiograph findings that show one bubble is in the stomach and the other is in the proximal duodenum and that little to no air is in the distal gut.

claims.text: The double-bubble sign can also be seen with duodenal web, annular pancreas and preduodenal portal vein; rarely, with complete duodenal obstruction from Ladd bands in malrotation
claims.quote: This sign can be seen with duodenal atresia, duodenal web, annular pancreas, and preduodenal portal vein. Rarely, it can also be seen with complete duodenal obstruction resulting from Ladd bands in a patient with malrotation.

claims.text: Prenatally suspected with polyhydramnios and/or a dilated stomach; prenatal ultrasound can detect a double-bubble sign (a large gastric bubble and a smaller proximal duodenal bubble) in up to 80% of cases
claims.quote: Diagnosis of duodenal atresia is suspected prenatally if there is polyhydramnios and/or a dilated stomach. Prenatal ultrasound can detect a double-bubble sign (a large gastric bubble and a smaller proximal duodenal bubble) in up to 80% of cases (2).

claims.text: An upper GI series gives the definitive diagnosis but must be done carefully by a radiologist experienced with this procedure in children to avoid aspiration and is not typically necessary if surgery is immediate; if surgery is delayed, a contrast enema should be done to confirm the double bubble is not due to malrotation
claims.quote: Although an upper GI series provides definitive diagnosis, it must be performed carefully by a radiologist experienced with doing this procedure on children to avoid aspiration and is not typically necessary if surgery is to be performed immediately. If surgery is to be delayed (eg, because of other medical issues, such as respiratory distress syndrome or the need to stabilize the infant), a contrast enema should be performed to confirm that the double-bubble sign is not due to malrotation.

claims.text: Causes Failure of canalization of the embryonic duodenum, which may be related to an ischemic event or genetic factors; the second most common GI atresia (estimated 1 in 10,000 live births)
claims.quote: Duodenal atresia is the second most common atresia of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. The estimated incidence is 1 in 10,000 live births (1). Duodenal atresia is due to the failure of canalization of the embryonic duodenum. This failure may be related to an ischemic event or genetic factors.

claims.text: Unlike other intestinal atresias, commonly associated with other congenital anomalies: approximately 25 to 40% have Down syndrome; others include VACTERL, malrotation, annular pancreas, biliary tract anomalies and mandibulofacial anomalies
claims.quote: Duodenal atresia, unlike other intestinal atresias, is commonly associated with other congenital anomalies; approximately 25 to 40% of infants with duodenal atresia have Down syndrome (1). Other associated anomalies include VACTERL (vertebral anomalies, anal atresia, cardiac malformations, tracheoesophageal fistula, esophageal atresia, renal anomalies and radial aplasia, and limb anomalies), malrotation, annular pancreas, biliary tract anomalies, and mandibulofacial anomalies.

claims.text: Symptoms Postnatally: feeding difficulties and emesis that may be bilious
claims.quote: Postnatally, infants with duodenal atresia present with feeding difficulties and emesis that may be bilious.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Once suspected: nothing by mouth and a nasogastric tube to decompress the stomach; surgery is the definitive therapy
claims.quote: Once the disorder is suspected, infants should receive nothing by mouth, and a nasogastric tube should be placed to decompress the stomach. Surgery is the definitive therapy.
